query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, continuous, and adherent ceramic coating to the surface of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can overcome its poor oxygen resistance limitation without sacrificing its useful mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Application of a thin, continuous, and adherent ceramic coating (e.g., alumina or zirconia) to the surface of the alloy
generation.conditions: Temperature: up to 1000 °C, Atmosphere: air or oxygen-rich environment, Exposure time: long-term (hours to days), Mechanical-loading boundaries: tensile loading at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1
generation.mechanism: The ceramic coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, preventing the formation of a thick oxide layer and reducing the degradation of the alloy's mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance, maintaining yield strength above 163 MPa and tensile ductility above 8% at 1000 °C
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of the ceramic coating in preventing oxygen diffusion and maintaining mechanical properties may depend on the specific coating material, thickness, and application method

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated alloy exhibits significant weight gain (>5%) or oxide layer thickness (>10 μm) after 100 hours of exposure at 1000 °C in air, and its tensile ductility decreases below 5% or yield strength drops below 100 MPa, then the hypothesis is falsified

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
